sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
July 2026 delivered a bifurcated global equity tape shaped by two simultaneous and opposing forces: a historic sell-off in the AI-and-semiconductor complex that crushed tech-heavy U.S. benchmarks, and a surge in energy and value names on the back of re-escalating U.S.-Iran hostilities that drove crude oil sharply higher. The S&P 500 gained a modest **+0.7%** for the month to close at **7,489.72**, lifted materially on the final trading day by Amazon's blowout Q2 report; the Dow Jones Industrial Average extended its winning run to a fourth consecutive month, adding approximately **+0.5%** to close at **52,485.03**. The Nasdaq Composite fell approximately **-3%** to close at **25,373.85** — but this headline figure understates the underlying severity: the Nasdaq-100 declined **-6.6%** and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index collapsed **-20.6%**, its worst monthly performance in years.

European indices outperformed meaningfully, with the FTSE 100 gaining **+4.0%** for the month — driven by its substantial energy weighting in BP and Shell — and the DAX advancing **+2.28%** to close near **25,800**, supported by energy, defense industrials, and chemicals. The CAC 40 closed near **8,486** (approx., verify before merging). APAC markets were the global laggards: Japan's Nikkei 225 retreated from June's close near **70,062** to finish at **64,362** — a monthly decline of roughly **-8%** — as Bank of Japan hawkish signaling and a technology rout weighed; the Shanghai Composite fell a sharp **-6.81%** to **3,832** as U.S. tariff escalation and property sector headwinds compounded.

The month's defining dynamic was the radical divergence between old-economy value benchmarks and the AI-driven growth complex that had dominated returns through Q1 2026. The S&P 500 Equal Weight Index outperformed the Nasdaq-100 by more than **7.5 percentage points** — the widest single-month spread on record between these two benchmarks — encapsulating an equity market in genuine leadership transition. Whether July's rotation proves a temporary de-risking event or the beginning of a more sustained regime shift toward value and energy will be the central debate for equity allocators entering H2 2026.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
AI Chip Reckoning & the Great Rotation -- The most seismic U.S. equity story of July 2026 was the collapse of the semiconductor and AI-chip complex, which had underpinned the Nasdaq's historic twelve-month advance. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOXX) plunged **-20.6%** for the month — its worst performance in years — following five consecutive losing sessions at the start of July and a broader investor reassessment of whether the AI capital expenditure supercycle would generate adequate near-term financial returns. Individual casualties were severe: Micron Technology fell as much as **-13%** in a single session, Intel suffered a brutal **-21%** decline over seven trading days, AMD shed **-7–8%**, and Samsung Electronics fell nearly **-7%**, with contagion spreading into Japanese and Korean technology supply chains.

The catalyst was a fundamental shift in investor sentiment from AI demand conviction to AI monetization scrutiny. With hyperscalers collectively guiding more than **$500 billion** in combined 2026 AI capex, markets demanded evidence that infrastructure investment was generating commensurate revenue acceleration — evidence not yet visible at scale in Q2 results. In this environment, equal-weight and value-oriented indices staged their best relative month in history: the S&P 500 Equal Weight Index outperformed the Nasdaq-100 by more than **7.5 percentage points** and the Nasdaq-100 Equal Weight by more than **5 percentage points** — the single best monthly outperformance since the Nasdaq-100 Equal Weight's inception in 2005.

For portfolio managers, the July rout raises a structural question: was the semiconductor sell-off a crowded-positioning flush that clears the way for a resumption of the AI trade, or a leading indicator of a genuine earnings disappointment cycle in technology? The dissenting view — that AI infrastructure investment will generate transformative returns over a 12–24 month lag — remains widely held, but the episode demonstrates how quickly sentiment can shift when technicals, valuation, and macro headwinds align simultaneously against a crowded consensus.

US-Iran War Re-Escalation & the Crude Oil Supply Shock -- The single most consequential macro event of July 2026 was the re-escalation of U.S.-Iran hostilities, with fresh American military strikes on Iranian facilities triggering immediate Strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions and reversing the post-ceasefire oil price normalization that had been the dominant macro tailwind in June. Brent crude surged sharply over the course of the month, approaching intraday highs near **$100/bbl**; on July 31, early-morning futures touched **$92.27/bbl** before retreating as a pause in U.S. airstrikes was announced overnight, with the closing price settling near approximately **$87.84/bbl** (approx., verify before merging); WTI tracked to approximately **$84.67/bbl** (approx., verify before merging). Goldman Sachs revised its Q3 2026 Brent forecast upward to **$95/bbl**, reversing the **$80/bbl** target set following June's peace framework.

The oil supply shock delivered an immediate stagflationary impulse to an economy already navigating above-target inflation and Federal Reserve vigilance. Airlines, chemical producers, and logistics companies that had rapidly reduced crude hedges following June's ceasefire news faced severe near-term margin compression with minimal buffer, and sell-side analysts began quantifying the Q3 2026 earnings guidance implications. Energy sector equities globally registered their best monthly performance since 2022, with U.S. E&P names and European integrated oil majors posting double-digit monthly gains.

For financial markets, the re-escalation has materially complicated the H2 2026 macro narrative. The Strait of Hormuz — through which approximately a fifth of global oil flows — remains partially disrupted, and any further deterioration in U.S.-Iran negotiations could push Brent back above **$100/bbl**, a threshold that would almost certainly force a Federal Reserve policy response and trigger a more abrupt de-rating of equity multiples. The episode underscores how fragile the June peace dividend proved and how quickly structural supply constraints can reassert themselves.

Amazon's $200 Billion Quarter & the Big Tech Earnings Season -- Amazon's July 30 Q2 2026 results delivered one of the most consequential single-stock earnings reports in recent memory: revenue reached **$200.6 billion** — the first quarter in corporate history to surpass the **$200 billion** threshold — on earnings per share of **$5.75**, far exceeding the sell-side consensus of **$1.82**. The EPS figure was materially boosted by a pre-tax gain of **$53.4 billion** tied to Amazon's investment in AI startup Anthropic; stripping out this mark-to-market item, underlying operating results remained exceptional, with operating income of **$27.5 billion** — up from **$19.2 billion** in Q2 2025. AWS cloud revenue grew **37%** year-over-year to **$42.2 billion**, the fastest rate in 18 quarters, as AI inference workloads and enterprise cloud migrations drove demand above the **$40.5 billion** consensus.

Amazon's beat was the headline of a broadly constructive Q2 earnings season for U.S. mega-cap technology, with S&P 500 operating earnings for Q2 2026 tracking approximately **+15%** year-over-year. The Amazon-driven surge on July 31 lifted the S&P 500 by approximately **+1%** on the final trading day, effectively rescuing the index from a materially deeper monthly drawdown. However, the market's reaction was notably muted relative to the magnitude of the beats: with Amazon raising full-year 2026 capex guidance to **$220 billion** — roughly **+50%** above 2025 levels — investors remain focused on a scenario where AI infrastructure investment will not generate commensurate revenue returns for multiple quarters.

For the broader tech sector, the key interpretive question is how to read the Anthropic gain: a **$53.4 billion** pre-tax mark on a private investment inflates EPS dramatically and flatters GAAP profitability, but it is non-cash and highly sensitive to Anthropic's next funding round. Investors focused on cash-generative AI monetization should strip out the one-time item and focus on the **37%** AWS growth and **$16.6 billion** AWS operating income as the true signal of AI demand strength. The result, on balance, validated the AI cloud monetization thesis even as it failed to resolve broader semiconductor sector anxieties.

Fed's Three Dissenters & the September Hike Risk -- The Federal Reserve's July 29 FOMC meeting produced no policy change, with the committee voting to hold the federal funds rate at **3.50%–3.75%**, but three policymakers — Cleveland's Beth Hammack, Minneapolis' Neel Kashkari, and Dallas' Lorie Logan — dissented in favor of an immediate **25 basis point** hike to **3.75%–4.00%**, marking the first three-way hawkish dissent since September 2016. The committee noted that headline inflation had cooled to **3.5%** in June but that core inflation at **2.6%** remained above the **2%** target, compounded by supply-side pressures from the crude oil surge and tariff pass-through. CME FedWatch subsequently priced a greater-than-**50%** probability of a **25 basis point** hike at the September 2026 FOMC meeting — a dramatic reversal from the cut expectations prevailing just one quarter earlier.

U.S. Treasury yields reacted meaningfully: the 10-year note climbed to approximately **4.67%** (approx., verify before merging) at the FOMC meeting date, and likely settled between **4.70%** and **4.75%** (approx., verify before merging) by July 31, while the 2-year yield settled near **4.24%** (approx., verify before merging), with a 10-2 spread of approximately **+45 basis points** as the curve steepened modestly. Real yields on 10-year TIPS moved above **2.3%** — a level that historically creates meaningful headwinds for equity multiples in technology and other long-duration sectors. Rate-sensitive sectors including REITs, utilities, and consumer staples underperformed the broader market materially.

For asset allocators, the prospect of a hiking cycle resumption in September — barely one quarter after easing speculation had dominated the consensus — introduces the risk of a more aggressive tightening trajectory than markets had assumed entering H2. The Fed's central dilemma remains unchanged: an energy-driven supply shock is inherently stagflationary, punishing real growth while simultaneously demanding a policy response that tightens financial conditions. The three-dissenter outcome signals that the committee is considerably less comfortable with current conditions than the headline hold suggests — and that any CPI upside surprise in August could tip the September decision firmly toward a hike.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
U.S. equity performance in July 2026 was defined by the starkest growth-versus-value divergence in recent memory. The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced approximately **+0.5%** to close at **52,485.03**, driven by energy sector leadership — major E&P and integrated oil names each gained double digits on the crude oil surge — alongside financial sector resilience and healthcare stability. The S&P 500 registered a modest **+0.7%** gain to close at **7,489.72**, with the equal-weight version outperforming the cap-weighted benchmark by a wide margin as energy and industrials dominated while mega-cap technology weighed on aggregate returns.

The Nasdaq Composite bore the heaviest losses, declining approximately **-3%** to close at **25,373.85** — but the full severity of the tech rout is better captured by the Nasdaq-100's **-6.6%** monthly decline and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index's historic **-20.6%** plunge. Individual casualties were dramatic: Micron Technology fell **-13%** in a single session, Intel declined **-21%** over seven trading days, AMD shed **-7–8%**, and Samsung Electronics fell nearly **-7%**. The sell-off reflected investor concern that collective hyperscaler AI capex above **$500 billion** for 2026 would not generate commensurate near-term revenue returns — a thesis the broader Q2 earnings season partially validated but did not fully resolve.

The decisive turning point came on July 31, when Amazon's Q2 2026 blowout — **$200.6 billion** in revenue, AWS growth of **37%**, and EPS of **$5.75** inclusive of a **$53.4 billion** Anthropic investment gain — catalyzed a broad market rally that lifted the S&P 500 by approximately **+1%** on the final trading day, effectively rescuing the index from a materially deeper monthly drawdown. The month's aggregate outcome — a fourth consecutive winning month for the Dow, Nasdaq-100's worst month since March 2025, and an S&P 500 eking out a marginal gain despite extraordinary intra-month volatility — is the clearest signal yet that equity leadership is rotating away from the mega-cap growth complex toward value, energy, and dividend-yielding sectors.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets delivered meaningful outperformance relative to U.S. growth-heavy benchmarks in July 2026, with energy sector strength and resilient industrial earnings driving positive regional returns. The FTSE 100 gained approximately **+4.0%** for the month — its strongest performance of 2026 — led by BP and Shell, both gaining double digits as Brent crude surged. The DAX advanced **+2.28%** to close near **25,800**, led by integrated oil companies, defense industrials, and chemicals; the CAC 40 closed near **8,486** (approx., verify before merging), with energy and industrial gains partially offset by weakness in consumer discretionary and automotive names.

The re-escalation of U.S.-Iran hostilities proved a structural tailwind for European large-cap indices given their significantly heavier energy sector weights relative to U.S. benchmarks. European defense industrials benefited from an additional layer of tailwind as NATO member nations accelerated procurement in response to fresh geopolitical instability, providing revenue momentum for Airbus, Rheinmetall, and BAE Systems. European banks were mixed: the prospective September Fed rate hike provided a net interest margin tailwind for cross-border operations, while higher oil-driven inflation raised concerns about consumer loan quality in Southern Europe.

Not all European sectors participated in the advance: automotive stocks declined on U.S. tariff uncertainty, with German OEMs particularly exposed to the new trade framework that took effect in July. The ECB maintained its policy rate unchanged at its July meeting, noting it would monitor energy price pass-through before adjusting its own path, and reiterated that its trajectory is data-dependent and independent of Fed signaling. July's European outperformance reinforces the structural case for overweighting energy, defense industrials, and financials within European equity allocations, while trimming exposure to auto and trade-exposed consumer names.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific equity markets delivered sharply divergent but broadly negative performance in July 2026, with both major regional economies registering notable monthly declines under distinct but intersecting macro pressures. Japan's Nikkei 225 retreated from June's close near **70,062** to **64,362** on July 31 — a monthly decline of roughly **-8%** — as the Bank of Japan's increasingly hawkish signals on rate normalization strengthened the yen and compressed the export-earnings multiple that had underpinned the index's exceptional year-to-date advance. A Samsung-driven technology rout in Korean markets spilled into Japanese semiconductor and electronics names, amplifying the pressure; notably, the Nikkei staged a **+4.03%** recovery on the final trading day as Amazon's earnings lifted global technology sentiment.

China was the clear regional laggard. The Shanghai Composite fell **-6.81%** to close at **3,832** — its worst monthly decline in over a year — pressured by U.S. tariff escalation, consecutive months of Caixin manufacturing PMI export-order contraction, and continued property sector deleveraging. The Hang Seng tracked broadly lower. The PBOC cut the reserve requirement ratio for select banks mid-month but refrained from broader stimulus, disappointing markets that had been pricing more aggressive easing given the deteriorating trade and growth backdrop.

The Bank of Japan's July language strongly implied a normalization move before year-end 2026, with USD/JPY approaching **161** as the initial yen-strengthening impulse failed to sustain appreciation against a dollar still supported by higher U.S. real yields. The prospective narrowing of the U.S.-Japan rate differential is a structural shift for global carry trades and regional FX volatility. Several major investment banks downgraded China equity outlooks to underweight during July, citing tariff uncertainty, property overhang, and reduced domestic policy space — a sharp contrast to European outperformance that encapsulates a global growth rotation expected to persist through Q3 and Q4.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
Currency markets in July 2026 were shaped by three competing forces: geopolitical risk-driven demand for U.S. dollar safe-haven assets, the inflationary impulse of higher crude oil prices, and growing expectations of a September Fed rate hike. The DXY dollar index oscillated within a relatively tight range, touching early-July highs near **101.39** before settling back toward approximately **100.5** by month-end (approx., verify before merging) as the immediate Hormuz risk premium partially faded and the Fed's July statement provided no additional catalyst to break the recent trading band.

EUR/USD held near **1.14**, as the euro benefited from energy sector terms-of-trade improvement in European current accounts while the ECB's July hold limited rate-differential widening. GBP/USD traded near **1.33**, with sterling supported by resilient UK labor market data and the Bank of England's continued hold. The most significant developed-market FX move was in the Japanese yen: USD/JPY approached **161** as BOJ hawkish signals proved insufficient to drive sustained yen appreciation against a dollar still supported by higher U.S. real yields, with yen carry-trade positioning remaining crowded and vulnerable to further BOJ language shifts.

Emerging market currencies experienced broad-based pressure in July, with CNY, INR, and MXN all weakening as tariff escalation triggered capital outflows from EM assets. The Chinese yuan's controlled but persistent depreciation reflects official tolerance for a weaker exchange rate as a partial offset to export volume losses from tariffs covering **99%** of U.S. trade partners. EM central banks in commodity-importing economies faced an acute policy trade-off: defending currencies against a weak domestic growth backdrop while import inflation from higher energy prices eroded real household purchasing power — a bind that severely limits their ability to ease policy in response to slowing growth.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
July 2026 was defined almost entirely by the crude oil market and the geopolitical events that drove it. Brent crude surged sharply over the course of the month, approaching intraday highs near **$100/bbl** following U.S. military strikes on Iran before the immediate risk premium partially unwound; on July 31, early-morning Brent futures touched **$92.27/bbl** before retreating as paused airstrikes were announced overnight, with the closing price settling near approximately **$87.84/bbl** (approx., verify before merging); WTI tracked to approximately **$84.67/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) at month-end. Goldman Sachs revised its Q3 2026 Brent forecast upward to **$95/bbl**, reversing the **$80/bbl** target set following June's peace framework.

Gold gained modestly to settle near **$4,043/oz** on July 31 — a near-record level supported by safe-haven demand, rising inflation expectations, and a broadly stable dollar. Gold briefly opened above **$4,100/oz** on the final trading day before retreating with oil as the paused-airstrikes news partially unwound the geopolitical premium intraday. The relative underperformance of gold versus crude reflects the headwind from higher real Treasury yields: with 10-year TIPS yields elevated above **2.3%**, the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion limits upside even in a risk-off environment. Copper closed near approximately **$6.49/lb** (approx., verify before merging) at month-end — supported by AI data center construction demand alongside supply disruptions from South American mining — having risen from approximately **$6.03/lb** in early July per LME cash settlement data.

For corporate earnings, the commodity moves in July carry two distinct second-order effects: a material earnings acceleration for global energy producers, and simultaneous margin compression for airlines, shipping companies, chemical producers, and consumer goods manufacturers that will crystallize in Q3 2026 guidance downgrades. The IEA revised its global H2 2026 oil demand forecast upward, noting that sustained supply disruption may require strategic petroleum reserve releases by consuming nations to partially compensate. The commodity complex delivered its strongest aggregate monthly performance in over two years, driven overwhelmingly by energy.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
U.S. Treasury yields moved meaningfully higher in July, as oil-driven inflation expectations and rising September rate-hike probability combined to push the curve upward across tenors. The 10-year Treasury note climbed to approximately **4.67%** (approx., verify before merging) at the July 29 FOMC meeting date — up markedly from the June 30 close — and likely settled between **4.70%** and **4.75%** (approx., verify before merging) by July 31, representing approximately **+20–25 basis points** of monthly move. The 2-year yield settled near approximately **4.24%** (approx., verify before merging), resulting in a 10-2 spread of approximately **+45 basis points** as the curve steepened modestly under long-end inflation expectations.

The Federal Reserve's decision to hold at **3.50%–3.75%** was expected, but three committee members — Cleveland's Hammack, Minneapolis' Kashkari, and Dallas' Logan — dissented in favor of an immediate **25 basis point** hike, the first three-way hawkish dissent since September 2016. With headline inflation at **3.5%** and core at **2.6%**, Fed funds futures ended July pricing a greater-than-**50%** probability of a **25 basis point** hike at September's FOMC meeting — a dramatic reversal from the cut expectations prevailing in Q2. The shift in terminal rate expectations drove a meaningful widening in 30-year mortgage rates, further dampening the housing recovery that had begun in Q1 2026.

Credit markets showed early signs of stress: investment grade corporate spreads widened by approximately **+15 basis points** and high yield by approximately **+40 basis points** over the course of the month, as energy-driven inflation and rate-hike risk combined to pressure leveraged balance sheets and increase refinancing risk for lower-rated issuers. European sovereign spreads — particularly Italian BTPs — widened modestly on oil-driven inflation pass-through concerns, while UK Gilts tracked Treasuries higher in yield. For fixed income allocators, the July repricing suggests a regime where neither the short end nor the long end provides a clear safe harbor, and active duration management will be a key performance differentiator through H2 2026.
